name: Tamoxifen

lead: Tamoxifen (Nolvadex) is a prescription oestrogen-receptor blocker for breast cancer. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is used off-label for gynecomastia and oestrogen control during steroid use, and some ask about growth-plate effects.
A review says it has been tried successfully in adolescent gynecomastia; no trials address its other cosmetic uses.

paras: It binds oestrogen receptors, blocking oestrogen's effect in breast tissue while acting like oestrogen in other tissues such as bone and endometrium.

The US label's boxed warning covers uterine cancers, stroke and pulmonary embolism; it also lists liver effects, hot flashes and fetal harm. Retinopathy and low platelets have been reported. Prescription-only.

lead: Tamoxifen, sold under the brand name Nolvadex among others, is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) taken by mouth. It acts as an oestrogen antagonist in breast tissue and as an agonist in some other tissues.[1][1] The US label (for the oral solution Soltamox) lists treatment of metastatic breast cancer, adjuvant treatment of early-stage ER-positive breast cancer, reduction of risk after DCIS surgery, and risk reduction in high-risk women.[2]

In appearance and bodybuilding settings it is used off-label, mostly to address gynecomastia and to manage oestrogen effects during or after anabolic steroid use.[3][4][5] Looksmax.org users also ask whether SERMs affect growth-plate closure, with threads citing conflicting laboratory findings.[6]
The US label carries a boxed warning for uterine malignancies, stroke and pulmonary embolism in the oncology setting, and warns of fetal harm and liver effects.[2] It is a prescription medicine.
infobox: UK 1973, US 1977 for advanced breast cancer (per Grokipedia)

paras: The label's approved indications are summarised above.[2] The 2015 patient-level meta-analysis of aromatase inhibitors versus tamoxifen, the SOFT and TEXT trials of tamoxifen with ovarian suppression in premenopausal women, and low-dose tamoxifen trials in breast intraepithelial neoplasia are among the large bodies of evidence.[7][8][9][10][11] An earlier systematic review examined adjuvant and neoadjuvant breast cancer treatments' effects on mortality.[12] Grokipedia describes off-label use in male infertility and gynecomastia.[1]

Gynecomastia is the chief appearance-related use. A looksmax.org user says they took tamoxifen for 20 days for gynecomastia, reported excess sweating only, and said it helped muscle gain; another says their gynecomastia hurts and hopes tamoxifen will resolve it.[3][4] A review on anabolic-steroid-induced hypogonadism lists selective oestrogen receptor modulators among management options for men with a history of non-prescribed steroid use.[5]

The boxed warning cites uterine malignancies (endometrial adenocarcinoma 2.20 versus 0.71 per 1,000 woman-years on placebo in the NSABP P-1 trial), stroke and pulmonary embolism, with fatal cases.[2] The label lists hot flashes, mood disturbances, vaginal discharge and bleeding, nausea and fluid retention as common reactions, plus embryo-fetal toxicity and liver cancer and abnormalities, some fatal.[2] Case literature describes tamoxifen retinopathy and thrombocytopenia.[13][14][15] These data come mainly from women treated for breast cancer; Grokipedia notes that thromboembolic risk has also been described in men.[1]

Tamoxifen is an oestrogen agonist/antagonist that competes with oestrogen for the oestrogen receptor, decreasing receptor-dependent growth signalling in breast tissue.[2] Grokipedia describes agonist activity in bone and endometrium.[1] Laboratory research has compared oestrogen receptor alpha and beta binding specificity.[16]

Grokipedia reports that tamoxifen was developed at Imperial Chemical Industries in the late 1950s and early 1960s as a potential morning-after contraceptive, failed in that role, and was repurposed for breast cancer; it was approved in the UK in 1973 and the US in 1977, and the FDA added chemoprevention in 1998 based on the NSABP P-1 trial.[1] The P-1 prevention study was published in 1998.[17]

Evidence in humans is chiefly in breast cancer: P-1 prevention,[17] the Early Breast Cancer Trialists' overview,[18] aromatase inhibitor comparisons,[7] SOFT/TEXT,[8][9][10] and low-dose TAM-01.[11][19] Registered studies cover other cancers, ovulation induction with clomiphene plus tamoxifen, and hepatitis C.[20][21]

No randomised trial of tamoxifen for gynecomastia in bodybuilders or for growth-plate effects in healthy adolescents was identified; the forum thread on growth plates cites laboratory studies with conflicting conclusions.[6]

On looksmax.org tamoxifen (Nolvadex) is discussed with testosterone and in gynecomastia threads.[3][4] A growth-plate thread quotes a cultured-bone study finding dose-dependent growth retardation and an in vivo study reporting that tamoxifen stimulated longitudinal growth in contrast to oestradiol; a reply says SERMs have mild oestrogenic effects on bone and advises against using them for that purpose without endocrinology expertise.[6]

lore.intro: Tamoxifen appears in gynecomastia and steroid-aftercare discussion and, less often, in questions about growth plates.[3][4][6]
